extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in mathematics or physics studying classical mechanics and dynamical systems
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter material and worked analysis for mechanical systems governed by central forces (Newtonian gravitation and generalizations), including definitions (conservative/central), conserved quantities, phase-space/energy-surface geometry, explicit solution (Kepler), reduction of the two-body problem, and blow-up of the collision singularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton's Second Law (mechanical system formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: m X'' = F(X). As a first-order system: X' = V, V' = (1/m) F(X); this is the standard second-order ODE model for a particle in a force field, called a mechanical system with n degrees of freedom on R^n × R^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat X(t) as a configuration-space trajectory and (X(t),V(t)) as a phase-space/state-space trajectory. Rewrite second-order equations as first-order systems to analyze existence, invariants, and flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configuration space and phase space
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution X(t) ⊂ R^n of the second-order equation lies in configuration space; the pair (X(t),V(t)) ⊂ R^n × R^n lies in phase (state) space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize phase space as the tangent bundle over configuration space; many invariants (energy, momentum) are naturally functions on phase space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dot and cross product identities (calculus tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: X·Y = Σ x_i y_i; (X·Y)' = X'·Y + X·Y'; cross product U×V = -V×U, |U×V| = |U||V| sin θ and (U×V)' = U'×V + U×V'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these identities for differentiation of energy, angular momentum, and for proving perpendicularity and plane-confinement results; apply chain rule and product rules in vector form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradient and chain rule for scalar potentials
rubrics_metrics.description: grad g(X) = (∂g/∂x1,...,∂g/∂xn). For F: R→R^n and g: R^n→R, d/dt g(F(t)) = grad g(F(t)) · F'(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to relate spatial derivatives of potential energy functions to force fields and to compute time-derivatives of potential/energy along trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative force field / potential energy
rubrics_metrics.description: A force field is conservative if there exists a smooth U: R^n → R with F(X) = -grad U(X). The associated system is called a conservative system; U is (a) potential energy (up to additive constant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The negative sign is conventional. Conservation of energy and Hamiltonian formalism apply; adding a constant to U does not change the force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinetic, potential, and total energy (first integral)
rubrics_metrics.description: For mass m and velocity V(t), kinetic energy K = (1/2)m |V|^2; total energy E = K + U. In conservative systems, E is constant along solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute E'(t) via dot-product identities and F = -grad U to show E' = 0. Use E to define energy surfaces in phase space and deduce motion constraints (e.g., zero-velocity curves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of Energy theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X(t),V(t)) is a solution of a conservative system, then the total energy E is constant along the solution curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: differentiate E = (1/2)m|V|^2 + U(X(t)), use V·V' = V·(1/m F) and F = -grad U to show cancellation. Use as a first integral to reduce dimensionality of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamiltonian formulation equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce momentum Y = mV and Hamiltonian H = K + U = Σ (1/2m) y_i^2 + U(x). The conservative system can be written in Hamiltonian form x_i' = ∂H/∂y_i, y_i' = -∂H/∂x_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This places the system in canonical Hamiltonian framework, showing H is conserved and enabling use of symplectic/phase-space techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central force field definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A force field F is central if F(X) is always a scalar multiple of X: F(X) = λ(X) X (often excluding the origin where field may be singular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central fields point directly toward or away from the origin; many physical examples (gravity, Coulomb) are central. Analyze motion symmetry and reduction to planar motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence for conservative central fields
rubrics_metrics.description: For a conservative force field F, the following are equivalent: (1) F is central; (2) F(X) = f(|X|) X; (3) F(X) = -grad U(X) with U(X) = g(|X|) (i.e., U radial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chain rule to relate radial dependence of U to F. When U depends only on |X|, the force is radial and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane motion under central forces
rubrics_metrics.description: A particle moving under a central force in R^3 always moves in a fixed plane (unless position and velocity are collinear, in which case motion is radial along a line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses constancy of Y = X×V (angular momentum vector). If Y ≠ 0, motion is perpendicular to Y and hence planar; if Y = 0 motion is radial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angular momentum and its conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Angular momentum is m (X × V). For central forces X × F(X) = 0, so d/dt (X×V) = 0 and angular momentum is conserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In planar coordinates angular momentum reduces to scalar L = m r^2 θ'. Conservation implies areal velocity constancy and underpins Kepler's second law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areal velocity / Kepler's Second Law
rubrics_metrics.description: Areal velocity A'(t) = (1/2) r^2 θ' equals constant along solutions of any central conservative force field (line joining particle and origin sweeps equal areas in equal times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from conservation of angular momentum L = m r^2 θ' (so r^2 θ' is constant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newtonian central force system (inverse-square law normalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitational (Newtonian) central force after normalization: X'' = - X / |X|^3, with potential U(X) = -1/|X|. The field is undefined (singular) at the origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study dynamics in configuration space C = R^2 - {0} (restrict to planar motion) and phase space P = C × R^2. Expect singular behavior as |X| → 0 (collisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-space energy surfaces and zero-velocity curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy surface Σ_h = {(X,V) | E(X,V) = h}. For h ≥ 0 each TX meets Σ_h in a circle of tangent vectors with radius → ∞ as X → 0; for h < 0 there is a zero-velocity curve r = -1/h separating accessible regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use energy relation (1/2|V|^2 - 1/|X| = h) to determine allowed velocities at each position. The zero-velocity curve indicates positions where only zero velocity is allowed at given energy (boundary of motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar-coordinate variables and energy/momentum formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: In polar coords V = v_r (cos θ, sin θ) + v_θ (-sin θ, cos θ) with v_r = r', v_θ = r θ'. Total energy: (1/2)(v_r^2 + v_θ^2) - 1/r = h. Angular momentum: L = r v_θ (= m r^2 θ').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express dynamics in (r,θ,v_r,v_θ) to exploit conserved L and reduce radial equation; substitute v_θ = L/r for further reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collision–ejection orbits for zero angular momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: If L = 0 (v_θ = 0), solutions (for h < 0 and inside zero-velocity curve) are straight-line radial motions that leave and return to the origin (collision–ejection) and reach the singularity in finite time due to |V|→∞ as r→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In TX ∩ Σ_h,0 only two opposite radial vectors (or zero on boundary) occur; use separable ODEs dx_k/dt = g(t) x_k to integrate to show X(t) scalar multiple of X(0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for circular orbit (special energy–angular momentum relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When L^2 = -1/(2h) (with h < 0), the quadratic in r has a single root r = -1/(2h) and vr = 0, v_θ = L/r, giving a circular closed orbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve energy relation with fixed r to find constant-radius solutions; sign of L determines orientation (clockwise/counterclockwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annular confinement and torus structure for nonzero L
rubrics_metrics.description: If L^2 < -1/(2h), radial motion is restricted to an annulus α ≤ r ≤ β (roots of quadratic), and the energy–momentum level set Σ_{h,L} is a two-dimensional torus (subset of 4D phase space) formed by two graphs over A_{α,β} joined at boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At interior r there are two possible v_r signs (outward/inward), joined at the boundaries where v_r = 0; use this to visualize invariant torus and to infer periodicity/quasiperiodicity properties of orbits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning-point behavior at annulus boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: At r = α (minimum radius) we have r' > 0 (so minimum), and at r = β (maximum) we have r' < 0; thus solutions oscillate in r between α and β while rotating in θ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute sign of r'' at roots using quadratic relation; shows that boundary circles are not invariant closed orbits (except special circular case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kepler's First Law (conic orbits)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Newtonian gravitation, solution paths with nonzero angular momentum are conic sections given in polar form by r(1 + e cos θ) = κ, with eccentricity e = sqrt(1 + 2 E L^2). The orbit is ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola according as E < 0, E = 0, or E > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by letting W = 1/r and obtaining d^2W/dθ^2 + W = 1/L^2 (harmonic oscillator with constant forcing). Solve and relate constants to energy and angular momentum to identify eccentricity and latus rectum κ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-body problem reduction to a central-force problem
rubrics_metrics.description: For two masses m1,m2 interacting gravitationally, let X = X2 - X1 (relative position). Then X'' = -g(m1 + m2) X / |X|^3 which is a Newtonian central force problem with different constants. The center of mass X_c moves linearly (X_c'' = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the relative central-force equation to obtain X(t), then integrate to recover X1(t), X2(t) using center-of-mass motion; alternatively use reduced-mass formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGehee blow-up of the collision singularity (r→0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce scaled variables ur = r^{1/2} v_r and u_θ = r^{1/2} v_θ and rescale time via dt/dτ = r^{3/2}; multiply vector field by r^{3/2} to obtain a new system without singularity at r=0, making r=0 an invariant manifold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blowing up replaces the singular point by a collision manifold (r=0) parameterized by θ, ur, u_θ. Solutions on this surface describe asymptotic behavior near collisions in original time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collision surface and energy relation in blown-up coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: In blown-up variables the energy relation becomes h r = (1/2)(u_r^2 + u_θ^2) - 1. On r=0 the relevant subset (collision surface) is u_r^2 + u_θ^2 = 2, a two-dimensional torus parametrized by θ and an angle ψ in the (u_r,u_θ)-plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict dynamics to r=0 to study limiting behavior of near-collision orbits; equilibria and invariant circles on this torus correspond to collision–ejection solutions and determine nearby flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamics on the collision surface (equilibria and slope)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the collision surface the reduced system yields ˙θ = u_θ, ˙u_r = (1/2)(u_θ^2), ˙u_θ = - (1/2) u_r u_θ (with dot w.r.t. rescaled time). There are two circles of equilibria (u_θ = 0, u_r = ±√2). Introducing ψ via u_r = √2 sin ψ, u_θ = √2 cos ψ gives dψ/dθ = 1/2, so non-equilibrium orbits have constant slope 1/2 in (θ,ψ)-coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these facts to classify unstable/stable manifolds of equilibrium circles and to understand how near-collision solutions wrap around the origin (typically change θ by ≈ 2π).

rubrics_metrics.name: Near-collision/near-miss dynamics and manifold connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Collision–ejection orbits correspond to heteroclinic connections on the collision torus; nearby noncollision solutions follow unstable/stable curves near equilibria on the torus, approach close to r=0, and then depart after θ shifts (e.g., by ±2π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret manifolds on blown-up collision surface to infer how families of near-collision orbits behave in original coordinates; use continuity and manifold theory for qualitative descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized blow-up for potential U = -1/|X|^ν (ν>1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For potentials U = -1/|X|^ν one uses scaled variables ur = r^{ν/2} v_r, u_θ = r^{ν/2} v_θ and an appropriate time rescaling to remove the singularity; analyze collision surface, bifurcations at ν=2, and structure of Σ_{h,L} for all ν>1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow analogous steps to McGehee transform; investigate how the geometry (collision surface, equilibria, bifurcations) depends on ν, with ν = 2 being a critical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anisotropic Kepler problem (µ>1) - modeling and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: System x'' = -µ x/(µ x^2+y^2)^{3/2}, y'' = - y/(µ x^2 + y^2)^{3/2} is conservative with potential U(x,y) = -1/√(µ x^2 + y^2). For µ≠1 angular momentum is not conserved; the collision surface is a 'bumpy torus' with equilibria and bifurcations (e.g., µ = 9/8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polar coordinates and McGehee-type blow-up to study collision dynamics; classify equilibria (sinks/sources/saddles) and their manifolds, and describe how trajectories approach/retreat near axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling with additional forces (glider example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example system with drag (opposite velocity) and lift (perpendicular) both ∝ v^2: θ' = v^2 - cos θ, v' = -sin θ - D v^2 (D≥0). Equilibria and their linearization classify flight regimes; for D=0 an invariant v^3 - 3 v cos θ exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates how to derive ODE models from force decompositions, analyze equilibria and invariants, and sketch phase-plane behavior; adding drag (D>0) changes qualitative dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises / explorations as procedural analysis steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter supplies explicit exercise tasks: write systems in polar coordinates, compute energy and momentum formulas, numerically investigate trajectories for h<0 and L≠0, perform blow-up transforms, compute vector fields on collision surfaces, and describe bifurcations and structure changes (e.g., at ν=2 or µ=9/8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises prescribe concrete procedural steps for applying the chapter's methods to generalizations and for practicing both analytic and computational exploration of dynamics near singularities.
